A hyperbola is the set of all points in a plane such that the absolute difference of distances to two fixed points, called the foci, is constant. It consists of two separate branches and is the most open of the conic sections, appearing in navigation, optics, and the graphs of reciprocal functions. The standard form for a horizontal hyperbola is x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared equals one. For a vertical hyperbola it's y squared over a squared minus x squared over b squared equals one. The two branches open away from each other, and the closest points are the two vertices on the transverse axis. The difference of distances from any point on the hyperbola to the two foci is always two a. The eccentricity e equals c over a and is always greater than one, making the hyperbola wider open than a parabola. The hyperbola has two asymptotes—diagonal lines that the curve approaches infinitely close to but never reaches. In navigation, the hyperbola appears in LORAN systems, where differences in signal arrival times from two transmitters place an observer on a hyperbolic curve. The reciprocal function f of x equals one over x and its generalizations graph as a rectangular hyperbola.
